title: Carini: Movies and a Mangusta

body_markdown:
I’ve owned or worked on several movie cars in my career. Cars can be a character in a movie, and I think the 1949 Buick Roadmaster in *Rain Man* is a good example. It’s a pivotal part of the movie and as much a star as Tom Cruise or Dustin Hoffman. *Rain Man* is my favorite film, but I’m biased because I’ve worked on this Roadmaster, and I have a daughter who is autistic, like Hoffman’s character, Raymond. The director, Barry Levinson, owns the Roadmaster, and my shop did a major restoration on it for him back in 2015.


Then there’s the Ferrari 275 NART Spider that Faye Dunaway drove in the original 1968 version of *The Thomas Crown Affair* , co-starring Steve McQueen. Most people don’t know how famous this 275 is, but Denise McCluggage and Marianne “Pinkie” Rollo raced it at Sebring in 1967. The pair were visiting Manhattan and stopped by to see Luigi Chinetti Sr., who was Ferrari’s U.S. importer at the time. This 275 had sat in the showroom for a while and Chinetti couldn’t sell it. When asked if he had a car they could race at Sebring, Chinetti said, “Take this piece of junk. Just bring it back!”


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


McCluggage and Rollo drove the 275 from New York to the race at Sebring in Florida. The car was completely stock except for a rollbar and fire extinguisher. McCluggage and Rollo placed second in their class and 17th overall—an amazing result. For the pit board, Denise and Pinkie used the piece of plywood that covered the spare tire in the 275’s trunk. I painted the car many years later, and the pit board was still in there with the chalk marks.


Shifting gears from film to real life, I had a great time at the Greenwich Concours showing a 1969 DeTomaso Mangusta my shop restored. I was there with the owner, Trent Newcomer. The Mangusta was built in Italy by Alejandro de Tomaso from 1967-1971. Mangusta is Italian for mongoose, which is supposedly the only animal that can kill a cobra. The name was meant to send a message to Carroll Shelby, as de Tomaso had fallen out with the creator of the Shelby Cobra.

>
>
> [A post shared by Wayne Carini (@waynecariniofficial)](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY2vJBtjPk1/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


Newcomer called me two years ago. “I inherited a Mangusta from my father, who recently passed away,” he told me. “I’ve known this car since I was 12 years old. It was the love of Dad’s life, and I’d like you to restore it.” We took on the car and did the restoration. When we finished, I called up Newcomer, told him I was going to show the Mangusta at Greenwich, and that I’d love for him to join me. He came and we unveiled the car for him right there on the show field. When the judges came to us, I told Newcomer, “Now it’s up to you. Explain what this car means to you. If the car has great family history and a great story, you have a good chance of winning.” Newcomer started telling the judges his story, tears rolling down his cheeks and he was choking up. The judges were very patient. They said, “Collect yourself for a bit.” He’d pause and then start up again. When the awards were later announced, I was right: The Mangusta won best in class.


> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY-QR1sn-CF/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
>
> [A post shared by Wayne Carini (@waynecariniofficial)](https://www.instagram.com/p/DY-QR1sn-CF/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


Moments like these are why I love my job. First, Newcomer was thrilled just to be at the concours. Then to take best in class the first time he showed his Mangusta, well, he was over the moon. Obviously, restoring cars is my business. For me, though, my reward is a customer’s reaction when they first see their restored car and how much they love it. It’s also a big reward when I see the owner or talk to them years later and they still love the car as much as the day it rolled out of our shop.
